The Community Well-Being index of a community

Source: R/indigenous_frameworks.R
cwbscr.Rd

Indigenous Services Canada's Community Well-Being (CWB) index: income, education, housing and labour force activity, each scored from 0 to 100, and their mean, from census profile figures.

Usage

cwbscr(
  incpercap,
  highsch20p,
  uni25p,
  notcro,
  nomajrep,
  partic,
  empl,
  bounds = c(2650, 75000)
)

Arguments

incpercap

Income per capita, in the dollars of the series' bounds.

highsch20p, uni25p

Percentages for education.

notcro, nomajrep

Percentages for housing.

partic, empl

Percentages for labour force activity.

bounds

The income bounds (default the 2016 and 2021 series: 2650 and 75000).

Value

A data frame, one row per community: income, education, housing, labour, cwb.

Details

The components, as the index's methodology sets them out (Penney, O'Sullivan and Senecal 2012; O'Sullivan and McHardy 2013; Indigenous Services Canada's reports on trends, 1981 to 2016 and 2021):

income

\(100 (\log y - \log a) / (\log b - \log a)\) for income per capita \(y\) (total income over total population) between the bounds \(a\) and \(b\) (2,650 and 75,000 dollars in the 2016 and 2021 series; 2,000 and 40,000 in the earlier ones), kept between 0 and 100 here.

education

two thirds of the percentage aged 20 and over with at least a high school certificate, plus one third of the percentage aged 25 and over with a university degree at the bachelor's level or above.

housing

half the percentage of people in dwellings with no more than one person per room, plus half the percentage in dwellings that need no major repairs.

labour

half the participation rate, plus half the employment rate of those participating (ages 20 to 64).

The index is the mean of the four. Indigenous Services Canada computes it from unrounded census microdata, scores only communities of 65 people or more and suppresses the components of communities under 250 people or 40 households: scores from published, rounded profile figures come close to the published index but need not equal it, and a small community's should be treated as the Department would. The full current methodology is available from the Department on request. The index measures socio-economic conditions as the census counts them; it says nothing of culture, language or relationship to land, and is not a measure of wellness as First Nations and Inuit define it. The CWB is Indigenous Services Canada's index, with bounds in the Canadian dollars of its series: for another country, set bounds in its currency and read the result as a CWB-style score, not comparable with Canada's.

References

Penney C, O'Sullivan E, Senecal S (2012). The Community Well-Being Index (CWB): Examining Well-Being in Inuit Communities, 1981-2006. Aboriginal Affairs and Northern Development Canada.

O'Sullivan E, McHardy M (2013). The Community Well-Being (CWB) Index: Disparity in Well-Being Between First Nations and Other Canadian Communities Over Time. In White JP, Peters J, Beavon D, Spence N (eds), Aboriginal Well-Being: Canada's Continuing Challenge. Thompson Educational.

Indigenous Services Canada (2019). Report on trends in First Nations communities, 1981 to 2016 (Community Well-Being index).
https://www.sac-isc.gc.ca/eng/1345816651029/1557323327644

Examples

# made-up profile figures for two communities, to show the computation
cwbscr(incpercap = c(18000, 31000), highsch20p = c(58, 81),
          uni25p = c(6, 19), notcro = c(71, 95),
          nomajrep = c(62, 90),
          partic = c(55, 68), empl = c(78, 92))
#>     income education housing labour      cwb
#> 1 57.30940  40.66667    66.5   66.5 57.74402
#> 2 73.57105  60.33333    92.5   80.0 76.60110
